Survey Links Medical Students' Artificial Intelligence Intentions to Habit and Fear

According to a cross-sectional investigation conducted among 391 undergraduate and postgraduate medical students at a top-tier university in China, intention showed a unique negative association only with ethical appropriation, defined as students’ willingness to use artificial intelligence beyond its intended purpose. The researchers extended the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2, known as UTAUT2, by integrating learner traits and specific attitudes toward artificial intelligence to capture the multidimensional nature of technology adoption in medical education.

The authors noted that artificial intelligence offers opportunities in medical training to enhance personalized learning and clinical reasoning. However, medical students differ substantially in whether and how they engage with these tools. While existing literature frequently treats artificial intelligence use as a single, uniform construct, the study team addressed this limitation by examining distinct appropriation dimensions alongside individual learner characteristics and psychological orientations toward technology.

To evaluate these relationships, the researchers administered a cross-sectional online survey measuring standard UTAUT2 constructs, Master Adaptive Learner traits, critical thinking, acceptance of artificial intelligence, fear of artificial intelligence, and technology anxiety.

Associations among the latent variables were estimated using structural equation modeling with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals generated from 2,000 resamples. Statistical evaluation revealed mixed overall model fit, yielding a scaled chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio of 1.83, a robust comparative fit index of 0.848, and a robust root mean square error of approximation of 0.051.

Within the structural equation model, behavioral intention was positively associated with habit, displaying a standardized path coefficient of 0.56, and performance expectancy, with a path coefficient of 0.30, while showing a negative association with fear of artificial intelligence at negative 0.16. At the latent level, behavioral intention correlated strongly with most appropriation dimensions, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.58 to 0.70. However, once habit, acceptance of artificial intelligence, and learner traits were entered into the analysis, intention exhibited no unique associations with these dimensions, except for the negative association with ethical appropriation at negative 0.33. Instead, several appropriation dimensions demonstrated direct associations with acceptance of artificial intelligence and Master Adaptive Learner traits. Furthermore, longer artificial intelligence use was associated with higher scores across all five appropriation dimensions, whereas a higher grade point average band was associated with higher integrative appropriation only.

The authors concluded that the extended UTAUT2 model may provide a useful structural framework for investigating artificial intelligence adoption within medical training. Because intention to use artificial intelligence was primarily tied to performance expectancy, habit, and fear, while specific appropriation dimensions connected directly to technology acceptance and Master Adaptive Learner traits, the researchers indicated that integrating artificial intelligence into medical curricula may require strategies that specifically target how students use artificial intelligence while actively aligning with core professional values, including critical thinking and self-directed learning.

Subject of Research: Adoption and multidimensional appropriation of artificial intelligence among medical students

Article Title: Understanding medical students’ adoption of artificial intelligence: an extended UTAUT2 model integrating learner traits and multidimensional appropriation

Article References: Li, Z., Meng, H., Qiu, R., Liu, Z., Song, R., Liu, J., Yuan, Q., & Cong, H. (2026). Understanding medical students’ adoption of artificial intelligence: an extended UTAUT2 model integrating learner traits and multidimensional appropriation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10781-y

Keywords: artificial intelligence, medical education, medical students, UTAUT2 model, technology adoption, Master Adaptive Learner, critical thinking, fear of AI, acceptance of AI, technology anxiety, performance expectancy, habit, ethical appropriation, integrative appropriation, structural equation modeling, cross-sectional survey
